# Abstract {.unnumbered .unlisted}

**Background**: Extreme heat may disrupt routine childhood vaccination by affecting access to health services and vaccination timing. This study examined the association between extreme heat exposure and the timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in Nigeria.

**Methods**: Data from the 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey were linked with temperature data for 2020–2024. The study included children aged 0–36 months and assessed timeliness of BCG, Pentavalent 1–3, Vitamin A and measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1). Heat exposure was measured using two approaches: a heatwave indicator based on a 5-day rolling temperature average, a 4-year return level and a 1940–2019 historical baseline, and a heat-index classification. Heat exposure was assessed within a 14-day window around the recommended vaccination date. Weibull accelerated failure time models were used to estimate associations between heat exposure and vaccination time, adjusting for selected demographic and socioeconomic characteristics. Model-standardized predicted vaccination coverage within selected timeliness thresholds was also estimated under different heat-exposure scenarios.

**Results**: BCG and Pentavalent 1 had the highest proportion vaccinated within 28 days of the recommended date (53% and 51%), while Vitamin A had the lowest (18%). Heatwave exposure was not clearly associated with vaccination timeliness, although point estimates generally indicated longer vaccination times for earlier antigens. In contrast, higher heat-index categories were associated with longer vaccination times for BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2, with weaker associations for later antigens. The direction of associations was consistent across the two heat-exposure measures.

**Conclusions**: Vaccination timeliness in Nigeria was sub-optimal, and the relationship between extreme heat and vaccination timeliness varied by the exposure measure and vaccination schedule. Earlier vaccines appeared more affected by extreme heat than later ones. These findings highlight the potential importance of considering extreme heat when planning and delivering routine immunisation services.
